# Section on Open Deposits <note>original: Upanidhi</note>

The king shall not compel the return of an <term>upanidhi</term> <gloss>open deposit</gloss> if it is lost or stolen by the act of God <note>natural disasters like fire or flood</note>, water, or by thieves. The loss of that property falls solely on the owner, provided there was no <term>jihma-karitam</term> <gloss>fraudulent action or negligence</gloss> involved. As **Narada** says: When a thing is lost together with the property of the bailee, the loss is the bailor's; the same applies to acts of God or the King, provided it was not caused by fraud.

The author states an exception to this:

### If there is loss after it was demanded but not returned, the bailee must pay the value and an equal fine. (66)

If the owner <term>margite</term> <gloss>asks for or demands</gloss> the return of the deposit and the bailee does not return it, then even if a <term>bhresha</term> <gloss>loss or destruction</gloss> occurs afterward by the King or other causes, the bailee must pay the value of the property to the owner and an equal fine to the King. (66)

Regarding the penalty for one who uses the deposit:

### One who uses it for livelihood by his own will shall be fined and made to pay it back with interest.

One who uses or transacts with the deposited property for profit without the owner's permission shall be fined according to the extent of the enjoyment or the profit gained. He must return the <term>upanidhi</term> <gloss>deposit</gloss> to the owner <term>sodayam</term> <gloss>with interest</gloss> if it was used, or with the profit if it was used in business. The rate of interest is stated by **Katyayana**: If one does not return a deposit, the remainder of a debt, a purchase, or a sale when demanded, it shall accrue interest at five percent <note>per month</note>. This applies when the item is consumed. However, regarding loss through negligence or ignorance, the same author shows a distinction: For what is consumed, he must pay with interest; for what is lost through neglect, he must pay the equivalent; for what is lost through ignorance, he should be made to pay slightly less. Slightly less means minus a fourth part.

The rules of open deposits are extended to borrowed items and others:

### This same rule applies to borrowed items, sub-deposits, trusts, and sealed deposits. (67)

**Borrowed items** <note>original: Yachita</note> refer to clothes, ornaments, and such, borrowed for festivals like weddings. A **sub-deposit** <note>original: Anvahita</note> is property placed in the hand of one person, who then places it in the hand of another, saying, Give this to the owner. A **trust** <note>original: Nyasa</note> is the act of placing an item in the hands of the members of a household in the absence of the master, to be handed over to him later. Handing it over in the master's presence is a **sealed deposit** <note>original: Nikshepa</note>. The word **etc.** <note>original: adi</note> includes gold and such placed in the hands of a goldsmith for making bracelets, and a **mutual deposit** <note>original: pratinyasa</note> where two people exchange items for safekeeping based on mutual need, saying, You keep mine and I will keep yours. As **Narada** says: This same rule is seen for borrowed items, sub-deposits, and the like; and likewise for artisanal work, open deposits, trusts, and mutual deposits. In all these cases, the same rules for return and liability as specified for open deposits should be understood. (67)

-> Thus ends the Section on Open Deposits. <-

***

<margin>
1. Another reading: that which results from fraud. 2. Another reading: one who earns a livelihood or enjoys the fruit. 3. Another reading: when being demanded. 4. Another reading: out of expectation, you keep this of mine.
</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the legal liabilities regarding various types of deposits and borrowed goods. It establishes that bailees are not liable for accidental loss unless they have been negligent, refused a demand for return, or used the property for personal gain.</summary>
